title: Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome in a Young Adult: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) is a rare, life-threatening variant of antiphospholipid syndrome marked by rapid multiorgan thrombosis. Early diagnosis remains challenging, especially in young adults.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 22-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia, Raynaud's phenomenon, and a recent cholecystectomy presented with headache, abdominal pain, and systemic symptoms. She developed thrombotic events in the brain, spleen, and kidneys. Laboratory testing demonstrated positive antiphospholipid antibodies, and renal biopsy confirmed thrombotic microangiopathy.
DISCUSSION: CAPS was diagnosed in the context of evolving systemic lupus erythematosus. Treatment included corticosteroids, plasma exchange, anticoagulation, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab. Despite delayed recognition due to overlapping autoimmune conditions, multidisciplinary management led to clinical stabilization.
CONCLUSIONS: This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of CAPS in young patients with autoimmune comorbidities. Early recognition and aggressive multidisciplinary treatment are essential for favorable outcomes.

title: Threshold of Hydroxychloroquine Dose Reduction Associated with Flare in Quiescent Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is recommended for nearly all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) unless contraindicated. However, concerns regarding long-term toxicity have led to increasing consideration of HCQ dose reduction or discontinuation. The threshold of HCQ dose reduction in clinically quiescent SLE remain unclear.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 381 patients with SLE in clinical remission (cSLEDAI-2K=0, prednisolone ≤5 mg/day, ongoing HCQ). The primary outcome was SLE flare, defined as ≥1-point increase in clinical SLEDAI-2K or treatment escalation. HCQ dose reduction during follow-up was evaluated using adjusted Cox proportional hazards models (aHR) for time-to-flare and adjusted logistic regression for flare occurrence (aOR). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis identified the reduction threshold.
RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 1.38 years, 52.5% developed flares. HCQ discontinuation was associated with increased flare risk (aHR 1.80, 95% CI 1.17-2.75; aOR 5.60, 95% CI 2.47-12.71). A ≥75% reduction was similarly associated with higher flare risk (aHR 1.53, 95% CI 1.02-2.30; aOR 4.40, 95% CI 2.17-8.92), whereas lesser reductions were not. Each 10% dose reduction showed a dose-response relationship in logistic analysis (aOR 1.13, 95% CI 1.06-1.21). ROC analysis identified a 74.7% reduction as an exploratory threshold for HCQ dose reduction (AUC 0.55).
CONCLUSIONS: In clinically quiescent SLE, HCQ discontinuation and substantial dose reduction (≥75%) are associated with increased flare risk. These findings support cautious HCQ tapering and avoidance of marked dose reduction.

title: Beyond Xerostomia: A Two-Year Follow-Up Case Report of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Health in Primary Sjögren Syndrome.
abstract: Primary Sjögren syndrome (pSS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by chronic salivary gland dysfunction that predisposes patients to oral complications and tooth loss. Although dental implant therapy has demonstrated favorable survival rates in patients with pSS, evidence regarding long-term peri-implant soft tissue health remains limited. This report describes the diagnosis of pSS following implant rehabilitation and highlights the impact of the disease on peri-implant health during a two-year follow-up. A 61-year-old man underwent implant placement at sites 14 and 16 with simultaneous sinus floor elevation and connective tissue grafting. Several months later, he developed progressive xerostomia, xerophthalmia, burning mouth symptoms, and dysphagia. Histopathological examination of a minor labial salivary gland biopsy revealed focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (Chisholm and Mason grade 3), with findings considered compatible with Sjögren syndrome in the clinical context. Following rheumatologic management with hydroxychloroquine and pilocarpine, the patient was monitored for two years. Clinical examination demonstrated persistent xerostomia and generalized gingival and peri-implant mucosal inflammation, whereas radiographic evaluation showed stable peri-implant bone levels without marginal bone loss. This case supports current evidence indicating that implant osseointegration and short-term survival can be maintained in patients with pSS despite chronic hyposalivation. However, it also illustrates that persistent salivary dysfunction and immune dysregulation may predispose peri-implant tissues to mucosal inflammation in the absence of radiographic bone loss, emphasizing that peri-implant tissue health should be evaluated independently of implant survival. Dental implants appear to represent a reliable rehabilitation option for patients with pSS when combined with individualized supportive care. Nevertheless, long-term success should be assessed not only by implant survival and marginal bone stability but also by careful monitoring of peri-implant soft tissue health. Early recognition of Sjögren syndrome by dental practitioners and multidisciplinary management are essential for optimizing both systemic and implant-related outcomes.
